body:
Ross wrote:

>sjj, you say you are in favor of unionism -- and are against 
>violence.  TK is *against* unionism and in favor of the destruction
>of industrial society.  It's not clear to me what ideas of TK's
>you support.  I expect he would not favor collective bargaining.
>

In fact, I never said I was in favor of unionism as it exists today. In an
argument about the air traffic controllers, I noted that many people today do
not have the opportunity to join unions. I asked how the air traffic
controllers' fight was different than the workplace battles many non-unionized
workers face. I never said that I found the current union system to be the
solution to the massive problems that corporate-industrial society has created.

In fact, I am in favor of the decline of the corporate industrial society. I
recall a time, not long ago, when it wasn't so invasive. I don't see that a
gradual return to a simpler lifestyle equates violence. I say it should be
gradual, because the state of our world got this way gradually, even though it
seems as if it happened overnight. It would be like the world going on a
"diet", not necessarily pleasant, but not a bad thing either, and for a very
positive goal.

TK stated in footnote 32, "It is even conceivable (remotely) that the
revolution might consist only of a massive change of attitudes toward
technology resulting in a relatively gradual and painless disintegration of the
industrial system..." I do admit that the possibilities of something more
devastating exist, but I think that my purpose is to find and work for the
easier solution, because I think that such a solution has a better chance of
being realized. In any case, most sane people will admit that the consequences
of our current trend will result in far greater devastation. Quite honestly,
the (human) world will probably not end in our lifetimes, but if the current
rate of growth and progress, (and human and environmental degradation)
continues,  it's not many generations off. And Ross, all those parks and golf
courses that you like will be sacrificed long before then.

In the face of the power of today's corporate power structure, the ability of
the individual to fight for himself is severely limited. I said, in the posting
you are refering to, that people who belong to a union have a little more power
against the corporate structure than the average person. I also bemoaned the
state of today's labor unions, which have become less representative of their
members and more representative of their leaders. In fact, I consider the
activists of the Hay Market Massacre to be much truer representatives of labor,
because these people were fighting for themselves, something I previously
posted on.

TK never said that people shouldn't fight for their rights. He did question the
motives of leftist groups, those engaged in struggles that personally had
nothing to do with them. I have less trouble with this portion of the manifesto
than some other people seem to have, because I have noticed that such types do
tend to be more concerned about the "having" of a battle than the actual goals.
So, in this sense, the current union structure is not much of a help, because
it has become part of the power structure. But I still cannot forget the labor
activities of the past, where the people concerned engaged in struggles for
their own rights. I am in favor of workers having their voices heard in battles
with the corporate rulership.

Of course, the corporate world has tightened its grip on society in the past
century, and have replaced governments as the real seats of power. There have
been so many buy-outs and consolidations of companies that it is impossible to
escape the corporate leadership of this world. Does this mean that ordinary
people should just sit back and take it?

I think that if people could feel that defending themselves sometimes works,
they will feel that their other goals could likewise meet with success. Many
people I talk to about various concerns of modern life seem more resigned to
rather than accepting of it. I don't think that the corporate lifestyle is
inevitable.

In the "Power Process" section, TK discussed the necessity for having goals. He
also said that it was necessary for people to attain some of their goals,
through their own struggle. Perhaps a successful fight against the corporate
world would enable people to tackle other personal battles. Many people relate
to the problems discussed in TK's book, even if they don't relate to its
author.

On your second point, I said that, like most people, I do not favor violence. I
never said that I didn't favor a radical solution, because I do. Radical and
violent are not synonyms.

I am encouraged by a new trend - increasingly popular books about living a
simpler life. This is a gentle kind of non-compliance that I find most
appealing. Titles such as "Inner Simplicity" and "Simplify Your Life" by Elaine
St. James, and "Simple Abundance - A Daybook of Comfort and Joy", by Sarah  Ban
Breathnach, preach the gospel of distinguishing between what you need, and what
you are told to want. They encourage people to stop recreational shopping, get
out of debt, don't watch too much TV, stop reading magazines (vehicles for
commercials), go to the library instead of buying books, etc. They also
encourage people to have fun, and not to do things they don't like. Quite the
opposite of the corporate message. These books are meant to be day by day
companions, not read at a shot, and then forgotten. Their message is that life
is too complicated but that you can do something to restore your tranquility.
Of course, if eveyone paid them heed, the consumer index would be in big
trouble. Ideas like these are a first step in a radical resistance at the level
of the people, which of course is what a grass-roots movement is.

There are also books about living a more self sustaining life-style, and
getting off the power grid. It does take a while for ideas to take root, but I
think we are just at the beginning. I am trying to spread the word that you can
be free, enjoy your life, connect to nature and live a happy life without
listening to or complying with the powers that be. I want people to know that
they can fight back.

I do not recall saying anything that was contrary to the basic ideas TK
expressed in "Industrial Society and its Future", but if I did, then I was just
building on them, and so much the better. TK hoped for a group of thoughtful
people to discuss the issues. It seemed to me that he realized the issues
deserved more thought than even one genius could provide. I don't think he
expected this thoughtful group of people to be "yes-men" to all of his ideas;
what's the point of a discussion in that case? I think this is why he expressed
doubts about some of his suggestions - it's a great strategy for getting
discussion going. His main concern is stated in the introductory paragraphs of
his book. The rest of it was a well argued, point following point, framework
for the discussion. That is what I want to be talking about!
